💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it.
  • According to recent reports, there are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so anyone can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, helping the home cook elevate their kitchen experience.

According to recent reports, there are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, plus sauces and cookbooks.

Seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

It has been revealed that A massive mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display shows how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

In a recent development, sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker highlights time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

According to recent reports, thermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

It has been revealed that A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

Freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

In a recent development, STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The manufacturer indicates the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT states it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Sources indicate that shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the manufacturer will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Industry observers note that someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Sources indicate that tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

According to recent reports, smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the organization’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

Cooking pancakes in a skillet is a solitary affair. If you’re the cook and don’t want to force cold coasters on everyone, you’re standing alone and eating last. Unless you have this new griddle, that is. This 12-pound rectangle spans two burners and stays put, providing an 18.5-by-9.8-inch cooking surface and two heat zones, so you can cook a bunch of pancakes, or eggs and bacon, simultaneously, which means everyone eats together. The carbon steel is nitrided, which means it resists rust and scratches without the need for questionable coatings. Plus, it arrives pre-seasoned with a surface that will only become more non-stick with proper use and care. Plus, a raised lip and rounded corners keep grease in while making it easy to pour off. It’s a great choice whether you’re cooking at the stovetop, in an oven, on a grill, or over a campfire.

Sources indicate that A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

According to recent reports, microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday indicates the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Industry observers note that green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow notes the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

Industry observers note that uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the massive chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

Industry observers note that A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water quickly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

In a recent development, most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

Sources indicate that so you know someone with a grinder, a pour-over cone, a French press, a cold brew pitcher, and a milk frother. But sometimes they need a coffee before they can face making coffee. And that’s where this indulgently overengineered Swiss superautomatic espresso maker comes in. The second-generation Z10 has a menu of 51 drinks you can choose and customize through the 4.3-inch touchscreen. Just pour beans into the hopper and fill the water tank. Drinks include classic hot options, as well as “cold brew,” which, while not true long-immersion, is still nice for ice thanks to unheated water pulsing through a coarser grind. With milk or without. But now there are also light selections, plus caffeine regulation levels, as well as sweet foam picks (with a $35 chocolate attachment sold separately). And the upgraded P.R.G.2+ grinder resets itself for each offering, dialing in optimized granule consistency so you never have to worry you’ll have bad luck with a puck. Sure, it’s a splurge, but think of all the time and space someone will save replacing all those other coffee contraptions.

Recent findings suggest that most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the organization calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one tech giant’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so plan on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

Recent findings suggest that nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the tech giant claims fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Recent findings suggest that boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum indicates it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Sources indicate that bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

According to recent reports, sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

It has been revealed that hexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad claims the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

In a recent development, detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Sources indicate that stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney indicates works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

According to recent reports, chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide notes it can go in the dishwasher, though the organization’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

According to recent reports, most microwaves cook by guesswork, and the most interaction you have is five beeps and the sighs/screams when things are too cold in the middle and hot at the edges. This sleek Japanese Microwave from Panasonic, however, uses its latest Genius Sensor 2.0 to constantly measure 64 points on your food’s surface every 0.1 seconds, so one button push can achieve even temperature throughout a plate of mixed leftovers. And steady inverter power ensures the center heats, too. The drop-down door, like a wall oven, suits even a narrow galley kitchen (aka many Asian apartments), while the flat, turntable-free interior can fit up to a 9-by-13 dish. This recent import is a 2026 Red Dot Design winner for a reason: it’s got a look as tasty as your bowl of steamy soup.

It has been revealed that want that perfectly fluffy restaurant rice at home, but without under- or over-cooking anxiety and hot-spot drama? Get a Zojirushi rice cooker. I’ve given the NS-ZCC10 Neuro Fuzzy Logic model as a graduation/housewarming gift multiple times because I knew from personal experience it delivers year after year. Then I got this pressure + induction cooker in 2025 and daaaaaaamn … somehow the best got better. Sticky-plump sushi or stir-fry grains, pleasingly textured oatmeal, brown rice that doesn’t take all of eternity. No sad, beige cement. This tiny, calm chef quietly adjusts the heat to deliver evenly cooked everything. It’s not as fast as some cookers, but it beats them in consistency. Fill to the line, press a button, go live life, come back to perfection. This is an upgrade that quietly, magically improves your entire kitchen rhythm.

It has been revealed that we’ve wasted so many herbs. You buy basil with such good intentions, but two recipes and three days later, there’s still so much that’s wilted and wasted. Same can be stated for other greens. And maybe you know someone in the same situation. One “simple” solution is for them to grow their own greens, but not everyone has room for a garden. And what about winter … Well, that’s where this egg-shaped enclosure comes in. Using NASA-inspired nutrient-infused fogponics (way more exciting to watch than standard hydroponics), anyone can grow lettuce or kale or cherry tomatoes, etc., from pre-seeded pods/reusable germination domes, and do it year-round. Just put the indoor garden in a side room, garage, basement, etc., (grow lights can get pretty bright), connect it to Wi-Fi with the Plantaform app, and give it water when an alert tells you. Then, in a few weeks, harvest time! Seasonings season! Garnishes galore! Just clean it well, and you’ll be able to keep good produce on the cutting board, not in the compost. Literally rinse and repeat.

Coffee nerds have so much in common with audiophiles. Both are obsessed with micro-calibrated gear and swapping components in and out in the pursuit of clarity. So if you know someone as obsessed with puck preparation as they are running a carbon-fiber anti-static brush over every album, you know someone who needs the Mazzer Philos premium light commercial single-dose grinder. Like a summit-fi digital audio converter, this $1,495 hand-assembled, heirloom-quality Italian appliance (available in black and silver) takes whatever beans it’s fed and extracts previously masked tasting notes with minimal morning commotion. A wide dial covers espresso to pour-over to batch brew coarseness, and the near-zero-retention vertical burr + chute knocker + Dose Finisher system lets you move between origins and brewing methods without yesterday’s beans staging a comeback. Swappable 64mm flat burrs give someone a chance to tune for vibrant light and full-bodied dark roasts, and the option to switch from stepped to stepless mode gives grind settings the same obsessive precision as establishing the perfect listening position.

South Korea isn’t a casual getaway. But you can still get some Seoul in your soul (food) at home with this set of sauces from three-Michelin-star chef Mingoo Kang of Mingles restaurant and James Beard Award winner Nadia Cho. Fermented slowly in onggi (traditional Korean clay jars that are buried in the hills), and branded with the Korean word for artisan, these sauces are so much better than the red plastic tub of industrial soybean-chili paste you’d pick up at the store (but I still got love for you, H Mart). Start by stirring the deep heat of cooking sauce into marinades, dressings, and/or broths, then use the finishing sauce to glaze meats, or drizzle some zest onto eggs, rice, or dumplings. Whether a chef you know prefers marinara or bibimbap, give them the gift of earthenware alchemy.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

  • Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that volkswagen introduced the ID. Buzz Beach, a fun spin on its electric van that’s built for camping and overnight stays. However, it won’t be cheap, starting at over $70,000.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

Industry observers note that the ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen stated it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

Sources indicate that for camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

In a recent development, the ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

Industry observers note that volkswagen will open orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

Recent findings suggest that what about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a new Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

Industry observers note that however, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

Breaking: Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC States

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.
  • The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year.
  • The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

Sources indicate that the fresh report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC mentioned that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), noted in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that at the moment includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:.

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”.

Industry observers note that “An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he stated.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”.

It has been revealed that “The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

According to recent reports, cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

Sources indicate that CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:.

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:.

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” remarked Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing newly introduced antibiotics is crucial.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#122154. Eagles are eating human-sized baboons in the Sahara desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (584 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Eagles are eating human-sized baboons in the Sahara desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • According to recent reports, new research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • It has been revealed that our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

According to recent reports, new research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

It has been revealed that our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

Sources indicate that in this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

Recent findings suggest that “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, noted in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

Recent findings suggest that with these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

In a recent development, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

Industry observers note that to defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what newly introduced ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

#122153. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1049 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is vital since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is vital since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Sources indicate that subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Recent findings suggest that both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

According to recent reports, the supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine stated.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

In a recent development, the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really key to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Sources indicate that some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine remarked.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he noted.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are key for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine mentioned, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh stated he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh stated.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: 5 Facts You May Not Know

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, millions of people line the streets of New York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible.
  • In a recent development, “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” states executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year.
  • Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, millions of people line the streets of New York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible. In honor of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Hoda Kotb, who has hosted the event since 2018, brought AD for a look inside the 72,000-square-foot studio where all of the floats, balloons, and costumes are designed and constructed. Read on to discover the most interesting behind-the-scenes tidbits that we learned.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

In a recent development, “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” states executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year. Before the Macy’s team moved into their current space, the magic happened inside a former Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, Upcoming Jersey.

Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.

In a recent development, the first parade in 1924 featured animals from the Central Park zoo, including elephants, lions, tigers, and bears. They were soon replaced with the giant character balloons that the parade is famous for today, but even that tradition used to look different. From 1928 to 1932, the balloons were released into the air and people were encouraged to find them for a cash reward. “That went on until things got a bit more challenging in the skies, because private aircraft would actually go and track them and try to grab them and bring them back down to Earth,” explains Coss. “But in 1931, there was a blue hippo that was released, never to be seen again. And this year, the blue hippo is making his triumphant return back to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.”.

In addition to the blue hippo, balloons of yore will be making a comeback for the 100th parade, including Felix the Cat, the first character balloon to appear in the parade, and Underdog, who hasn’t made an appearance at the parade in 42 years. Snoopy, the most frequently recurring balloon, will return this year as his alter ego Joe Cool for the first time.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

“The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been in production since my first day here, five years ago,” says Coss. “This year the stakes are high; you only have one shot at the 100th.” To mark the occasion, there will be seven latest balloons, six new floats, and one new “balloonicle,” or balloon vehicle.

Hoda Kotb welcoming AD to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

According to recent reports, from concept drawings to weatherproofing, it can take up to six months to complete a parade float. “While a lot of the work here requires a lot of planning, a lot of design, a lot of engineering, our end goal is to bring people together, to inspire joy, to create that new tradition,” states Coss, “whether it’s a family experiencing it for the first time or experiencing it for the 25th time.”.

#122148. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your upcoming favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered issue, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

Sources indicate that so when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Sources indicate that ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

Industry observers note that the options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

Industry observers note that the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

According to recent reports, harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

Sources indicate that if you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Sources indicate that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

It has been revealed that the idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he mentioned, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

In a recent development, unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

According to recent reports, in the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

According to recent reports, george Papanicolaou moved to New York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

His wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

It has been revealed that in 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It has been revealed that it took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the conversion of the automotive industry over to electric vehicles, sold as a foregone conclusion by many car brands in the early 2020s, may have largely stalled out in America, but the picture is far different globally. According to data from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, EVs now account for 31 percent of all passenger vehicle sales.

It has been revealed that and the global increase came despite falling sales in China. The major driver of electric vehicle sales has been Europe; European EV sales have risen 37 percent year over year so far in 2026, climbing to 43 percent of the new vehicle sales market. CommBank data also revealed substantial growth rates in countries such as Brazil (EV sales up 164 percent, to a 13 percent market share) and India (EV sales up 76 percent, to a 9 percent market share). Even in Japan, where manufacturers have been notably EV-reticent, sales jumped 80 percent year-over-year to 5 percent of the market.

In a recent development, meanwhile, electric vehicle sales have declined in the United States this year. According to Cox Automotive data, EV sales made up 6.4 percent of the new car market in Q3 of 2026, down from more than 10 percent in Q3 of 2025. Fuel prices have been elevated this year, but that has led Americans to gravitate toward hybrids rather than fully electric vehicles. Total electrified vehicles now account for nearly 25 percent of the American market.

Industry observers note that much of the decline has been a direct result of Trump administration policies. Last year, the U.S. eliminated a $7500 federal tax credit for electric cars, which—due to a commercial vehicle loophole—made them especially cheap for buyers to lease; the 10 percent share of sales in Q3 2025 came from a glut of sales as buyers rushed to take advantage of the tax credits before they expired. Congress is also considering imposing an annual federal tax on electric cars.

In a recent development, the Trump administration has also effectively eliminated enforcement of America’s CAFE standards, which would have effectively forced manufacturers to sell EVs to avoid hefty fines. American laws and tariffs also effectively prohibit importing affordable Chinese-made EVs, which have been a major reason behind the sales increase in Europe.

Industry News: Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took glitch with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

It has been revealed that A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered latest approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

In a recent development, “I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup remarked in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

Recent findings suggest that it took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Sources indicate that instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen mentioned this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

In a recent development, “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

Sources indicate that but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” remarked Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

In a recent development, okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he remarked. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

Recent findings suggest that “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Firm, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Recent findings suggest that alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Presently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.
